size.note: Wikipedia, citing Seabra (1900), gives single figures, not ranges: head-and-body length 40 mm, tail 32 mm, ear 11 mm and forearm 35 mm. Those values are entered here as identical min and max bounds. No mass or shoulder height was published on the pages used. Skinner and Chimimba (2005, p. 299) give, in Table 177.1 (all samples combined): mass 0.0031–0.0057 kg.

summary: A small insect-eating vesper bat of savanna and woodland, often found near water. The 2016 regional assessment rates it Least Concern and lists it as present in Kruger National Park. That assessment, which uses the name Hypsugo anchietae, does not describe a seasonal or migratory pattern, so the Kruger animals are treated as year-round residents. Fur colour and roost sites were not described on the pages used.
description: A small vesper bat. Wikipedia, citing the 1900 description, gives a head-and-body length of 40 mm, a tail of 32 mm, an ear of 11 mm and a forearm of 35 mm. No coat colour, ear shape or other field marks were published on the 2016 regional assessment or the Wikipedia page used here. This file keeps the checklist name Neoromicia anchieta. The 2016 assessment treats the species as Hypsugo anchietae and states that the correct spelling of the epithet is anchietae, not anchieta or anchietai. Wikipedia places it in Neoromicia as N. anchietae, formerly in Pipistrellus, and says phylogenetic evidence supports that genus transfer.
habits: The 2016 assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2010), says very little research is available on feeding ecology and roosting behaviour, but the species is considered a clutter-edge and clutter forager, and animals are often collected when nets and harp traps are placed above water. In Durban it has been found along rivers in urban landscapes (Naidoo et al. 2011). The same assessment states that there are no data on the types of roosting sites used. No migrant or seasonal movement pattern is given.

diet.summary: An insectivore. At the Sudwala Caves in Mpumalanga, the diet was found to comprise Hemiptera, Diptera and Coleoptera (Schoeman 2006, cited in the 2016 assessment).

young: The 2016 assessment says little is known of reproductive biology. In KwaZulu-Natal, a female pregnant with two fetuses was recorded in October (Kearney and Taylor 1997). Pup appearance and Kruger breeding months were not published on the pages used.

prey.note: The 2016 assessment, citing Schoeman (2006), reports a diet of Hemiptera, Diptera and Coleoptera at the Sudwala Caves in Mpumalanga. Not mammals in this guide.

habitat: The 2016 assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2010), says the species is typically associated with dry and moist savannah and woodland. Specimens in KwaZulu-Natal were collected from woody habitats such as Afromontane forest, riparian forest, coastal forest or bushveld (Taylor 1998). Wikipedia, citing Kingdon et al. (2013), adds riparian habitats, coastal and scrub forests, and the Bushveld ecoregion, often near open water. No Kruger-specific habitat account was found.

population.notes: No Kruger census or SANParks park-wide count was found. The 2016 regional assessment lists the current population trend as Unknown, gives no Kruger figure, and, citing ACR (2015), says the species is considered locally common in southern Africa though predominantly collected from only a few localities (Monadjem et al. 2010). Number of mature individuals is listed as Unknown.

research.note: This file follows species-list.json in treating the Kruger-list animal as Neoromicia anchieta (English Anchieta's bat; Afrikaans Anchieta se vlermuis) and does not remap the name. The 2016 regional assessment uses Hypsugo anchietae, lists Pipistrellus anchietae as a synonym, and states that the correct spelling is anchietae, not anchieta or anchietai; it places the species in Hypsugo on bacular and chromosomal evidence. Wikipedia and later phylogenetic papers cited there support a transfer to Neoromicia under the spelling N. anchietae. iNaturalist taxon 1431023 is Neoromicia anchieta (preferred English name Anchieta's Serotine Bat) and lists Pipistrellus anchietai, Pipistrellus anchietae and Hypsugo anchietae as invalid names; that English form is flagged here, not used to change the checklist name. These are genus transfers and a spelling difference, not a split. No 2025 EWT project page was listed on the Chiroptera tag pages or in the red-list table, which links only the 2016 PDF.

gaps: No 2025 EWT project page was found; conservation, habitat, diet and the Kruger record are taken from the 2016 assessment (Hypsugo anchietae).
No coat colour, ear shape or other field marks were published on the pages used, so the adult variant marks are all null.
No published mass, shoulder height, or measurement ranges; only single 1900 description figures for head-and-body, tail, ear and forearm are available.
No Kruger census or park-wide count; the 2016 assessment lists the regional trend as Unknown and discusses southern African abundance, not a Kruger figure.
Roost sites are undocumented in the sources used.
No sourced echolocation or social-call description. No iNaturalist sound was found in Kruger (place 69020).
No licensable photograph in Kruger (place 69020) or South Africa (place 6986); iNaturalist taxon 1431023 had no observations.

Gap-fill: iNaturalist taxon 1431023 still has no licensed research-grade photographs in southern Africa (place 113055). Wikimedia Commons searches for Neoromicia anchieta and Hypsugo anchietae returned only museum skulls and range maps.
Pup appearance was not published in the sources used.
Predators were not identified in the sources used.
